newsitem.title: FRANCE: French conscription marches towards scrap-heap.
newsitem.headline: French conscription marches towards scrap-heap.

text.p: France's military conscription marched a step closer to the scrap-heap on Tuesday with a parliamentary debate on a controversial bill which would replace it with a five-day civic lecture.

The plan, which involves abolishing conscription in 2002, is part of a move towards all-professional armed forces designed to modernise the military and increase its capacity for long-term action overseas.
Both opposition Socialists and members of the centre-right UDF, junior partner in the ruling coalition, have criticised Defence Minister Charles Millon's reform of military service.
"It's quite normal that the end of military service should prompt nostalgia," Millon said in an interview on RTL radio.
But he added: "We have to set up defences which correspond to our needs -- we have to move to a professional army."

Opposition and government deputies of the National Assembly, the lower house, have pushed through 139 amendments for debate, starting at 1500 GMT. One provides for conscription to be reinstated at any time if necessary.

Asked whether the government would accept such changes, Millon answered: "Conscription hasn't been abolished in the bill. It still exists. We're creating a new system which will allow...young people to commit themselves voluntarily."

Conscription, dating back to 1793, involves more than 400,000 men every year. Its duration was gradually cut to under a year as it became increasingly unpopular among many young men who felt they were wasting time which should be spent looking for jobs.

The bill says all young people would be subject to a census at the age of 16 and would be summoned to a five-day "rendez-vous citoyen" (civic meeting) -- a course on Republican institutions and defence -- between 18 and 25.

Volunteers aged 18 to 30 could enlist for national service lasting between nine months and two years, either in the armed forces, as civilian social workers in France and overseas territories, or abroad in humanitarian and development work.
The choice is between "service in a track-suit and service in combat gear", grumbled Gaullist Jacques Baumel, adding that he had many doubts about "this ersatz conscription".

Several senior army officers have privately criticised the new civic meetings as too little and costing too much: an estimated 1.8 billion francs ($360 million) a year -- almost the price of a second French nuclear-powered aircraft-carrier over the six years of the defence procurement budget.
Far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen has blasted the civic meetings as intended to conceal a dismantling of France's armed forces after the Cold War.

The ruling coalition, with a big majority in parliament, is expected to push the reform through after a three-day debate. But the Assembly's defence commission has already changed the bill to stress defence is the main aim of the civic meetings and that conscription is only suspended.
The civic meetings would start this year for men and in 2003 for women.

Under an overhaul ordered by President Jacques Chirac last February, France's overall military strength will drop from half a million to 350,000 when the move to all-professional forces is completed in 2002. The number of troops serving abroad will be cut to 39,000 from 56,000.
